source.title: Sparse Autoencoders for Sequential Recommendation Models: Interpretation and Flexible Control
source.authors: Anton Klenitskiy; Konstantin Polev; Daria Denisova; A. Vasilev; Dmitry Simakov; G. Gusev

record.file_problem: None; the full paper text, including appendices, is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study applies sparse autoencoders to sequential recommendation models to interpret and control their recommendations. It does not test superposition, feature-capacity competition, or whether SAE features are complete, stable, canonical units.
record.gate_note: The paper reports SAE-feature interpretability metrics, comparisons with transformer neurons, and recommendation changes after steering. These are relevant to SAE representations in recommenders, but do not test the listed claim versions. The Toy Models of Superposition reference is cited, not tested. Results from other cited studies are not included.
record.test_reason: The study applies L1 SAEs to small sequential-recommendation transformers (GPTRec, BERT4Rec; hidden size 64) to interpret and steer them. It reports attribute-correlation metrics, SAE-versus-neuron comparisons and steering effects on recommendations. None of this tests toy-model geometry (V1), capacity competition (V2) or non-capacity polysemanticity (V3). V4 names LLMs, and these are recommender models trained from scratch on interaction data, so the SAE-versus-neuron result is a different kind of system. Completeness, stability and canonicality of SAE features (V5) and feature dimensionality (V6) are not measured. Toy Models of Superposition is only cited.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct: the authors conclude SAEs learn meaningful, interpretable, largely monosemantic features in sequential recommenders, and that steering these features flexibly controls recommendations consistent with their interpretations.
record.recipe_differences: Applies L1 sparse autoencoders to recommendation-model activations and steers their features; it does not reproduce the Toy Models of Superposition method or its geometry experiments.
record.method_sensitivity: L1 regularization strongly affects reconstruction, sparsity, and recommendation metrics. The paper selects L1=0.1 and dictionary size 2048; for fixed L1, reconstruction error is stable for dictionary sizes 512–8192, and active-feature counts are stable for sizes 1024–8192. The first transformer block has slightly better interpretability metrics, though other layers give similar results. Interpretability metrics fluctuate across runs; five runs are averaged for the parameter-sweep plot.

fits_no_version.finding: In recommender transformers, top SAE features correlate with genres and other item attributes about twice as strongly as top layer neurons. Mean correlation is 0.44 vs 0.20 for GPTRec-ML, 0.29 vs 0.14 for BERT4Rec and 0.32 vs 0.16 for Music4All. Pop is an exception where neurons do better.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In small sequential-recommendation transformers, SAE features are more attribute-aligned (monosemantic) than individual layer neurons.

fits_no_version.finding: Steering a single SAE feature shifts the proportion of the corresponding genre monotonically. The exception is the BERT4Rec 'Western' feature, which mainly raised War. SAE steering is comparable to linear-probe steering.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Steering SAE features in recommender transformers controls the corresponding attribute in outputs, but depends on whether a matching feature was learned.

record.problems: The evidence concerns two recommendation architectures and two datasets, not LLMs or toy superposition networks. Most control-curve values are presented in figures without exact numbers in the text. The paper notes run-to-run fluctuations in interpretability metrics but does not report error bars or other uncertainty estimates for the tabulated results.
record.rows_left_out: No separate rows for each genre-specific metric, SAE activation value, or recommendation-quality curve; these are numerous, often figure-only, and do not test the listed claim versions. Aggregate feature-correlation results and the text-described control outcomes are retained.

untested.parts: All: no toy networks, no sparsity-dependent phase transition, no feature geometry.
All: no test of capacity competition or of important features getting dedicated dimensions.
All: no test of polysemanticity arising without capacity pressure.
All for LLMs. An analogous SAE-versus-neuron comparison exists only for recommender transformers.
Completeness, stability across seeds or sizes, and canonicality are not measured. Run-to-run fluctuation of mean correlation is noted only qualitatively.
All: 1-D versus multi-dimensional features are not compared.

record.verdict_notes: Borderline case. Read loosely as 'real models', V4 could arguably cover the SAE-versus-neuron comparison, but V4 specifies LLMs and these are tiny recommender models, so rows are left at none. Results not recorded as rows, all outside the claim versions: Appendix C Table 6 compares SAE features with neurons for actor, company, country and director (e.g. actor mean 0.51 vs 0.15). The linear-probe comparison has mean probe correlation 0.7. Section 7.2.2 gives a qualitative example of feature granularity: a 'Star Wars' series feature alongside separate non-overlapping single-episode features. That example hints at the non-canonical dictionaries relevant to V5 but is not measured as such.

versions.untested_parts: Does not test superposition geometry, sparsity-dependent transitions, or regular geometry in toy networks.
Does not test capacity competition, dedicated dimensions for important features, or feature sharing due to limited capacity.
Does not test whether polysemanticity can arise without capacity pressure.
Studies sequential recommendation transformers, not LLMs; does not test whether LLM features spread across neurons or are recovered by SAEs.
Measures attribute alignment and steering effects, but does not test whether SAE features are complete, stable, or canonical units.
Does not compare one-dimensional feature directions with multidimensional features.

rows.subject: GPTRec
rows.operation_detail: Set one selected SAE feature activation at the last sequence step to values swept from -10 to 10, then measured recommendation genre proportions.
rows.measure: Proportion of genres in top-10 recommendations
rows.value: The corresponding genre proportion increases monotonically with activation; it is close to zero at large negative activations and reaches very high values at large positive activations.
rows.note: Outcome is described in the text; exact curve values are shown only in the figure.

rows.subject: BERT4Rec
rows.operation_detail: Modified one selected SAE feature activation and measured recommendation genre proportions.
rows.value: Action, Sci-Fi, Fantasy, and Children proportions change as expected; modifying the Western feature substantially increases War, while Western itself is not strongly affected.
rows.locator: Appendix A, Figure 12 and accompanying text
rows.note: The paper interprets the Western result as indicating that the feature is associated with War and that no meaningful Western feature was learned.

rows.subject: GPTRec
rows.operation_detail: Set one selected SAE feature activation at the last sequence step to values swept from -10 to 10, then measured recommendation genre proportions.
rows.value: The corresponding genre proportion increases monotonically with activation, is near zero for large negative activations, and reaches high levels for large positive activations.
rows.locator: Appendix B, Figure 14 and accompanying text
rows.note: The text also describes cross-genre changes consistent with the feature correlations; exact curve values are shown only in the figure.
